# About this document {.unnumbered}

This document is a reference analysis for the author, not a course page. It shows what
students could do with the cocoa allometry data with the tools of Chapters 1 to 7 (RTMB,
RTMBdist, DHARMa and TMB), and follows the structure of the analyses in
`Case Studies/Adalia` and `Case Studies/Infiltration`: the data, an exploration, the
model, the choice of curve, distribution and random effect, the candidates for the effect
of management, the answer, checks of the model, an extension to tree height and a
simulation of the estimator. Alternatives are in boxes titled "Alternative" and traps in
boxes titled "Pitfall"; @sec-summary lists them all. `README.md` in this folder describes
the sources of the data and what is still not known about them; `data_description.md`
describes the study for students.

The data come from an unpublished manuscript by Goudsmit et al., which fitted cubic
polynomials of the logarithm of the diameter with `lme4` and added management as
predictors. Its Figure 3, aboveground biomass against stem diameter for four management
scenarios, is the figure that this analysis tries to improve on (@sec-figure3).

::: {.callout-note title="Possible research question (for the author to decide)"}
Does the relation between stem diameter and aboveground biomass of cocoa trees differ with
management (shade, planting density), and can these data show it? The answer below is the
typical mean aboveground biomass of shaded and of unshaded trees with stem diameters of 4
and 16 cm, both inside the range of the shaded and of the unshaded trees, the ratio
between the two, and the same quantities per site.
:::

The document needs RTMB, RTMBdist, DHARMa, TMB and knitr and takes about one minute to
render, most of it in the simulation of @sec-simulation. The optimisations are
deterministic and every simulation has its own seed. Numbers in the text are calculated
inline from the code, except descriptions of what a figure shows, which were written from
the figures of the run of 25 November 2026 (R 4.6.1).

Status: generated draft (25 November 2026), not reviewed by the author.

# The data {#sec-data}

Cocoa (*Theobroma cacao*) trees were harvested in 12 fields at four sites (Table 1 of the
manuscript): a research station near Divo in Côte d'Ivoire (CIV1; fields of 1.5, 5, 10 and
19 years), a research centre at Tiassalé in Côte d'Ivoire (CIV2; trees of 2 and 3.25
years), a commercial farm in the province of Guayas in Ecuador (ECU; 1, 6 and 11 years)
and the Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria at Ibadan (NGA; 8, 12 and 47 years). Before
harvest, the stem diameter was measured 20 cm above the ground and the height of the tree
from the ground to its highest point; the tree was then cut and separated into wood and
leaves, and their dry mass determined from subsamples. Aboveground biomass (AGB) is the sum
of the wood and the leaves. The sites differ in planting material (CCN51 in Ecuador, hybrid
mixtures in Côte d'Ivoire, TC series and Amazon mixtures in Nigeria), climate and
management; the Ecuadorian trees are hedged and irrigated.

The file `allometry.csv` has one row per tree: the tree code (`tree`), the site, the field
(`field`, site and age), the age (`age_years`), the diameter at 20 cm (`dia20_cm`), the
height (`height_m`), the dry masses of wood, leaves, aboveground biomass and roots (kg),
and the management of the field: shade trees (`shade`, yes or no), planting density
(`density_ha`, trees/ha), irrigation and fertilisation (yes or no). `make_allometry_csv.R`
builds it from the spreadsheet `CocoaAllometry.xlsx`.

```{r}
allo = read.csv("allometry.csv")
str(allo[, c("tree", "site", "field", "age_years", "dia20_cm", "height_m", "wood_kg",
             "leaf_kg", "agb_kg", "shade", "density_ha", "irrigation", "fertilisation")])
```

The factors get explicit levels (the reference level first), the fields are ordered by
site and age as in the file, and the planting density is centred at 1,200 trees/ha and
expressed in hundreds of trees/ha (`density_100`), so that its coefficient is the change
for 100 trees/ha more.

```{r}
allo$site = factor(allo$site)
allo$field = factor(allo$field, levels = unique(allo$field))
for (v in c("shade", "irrigation", "fertilisation")) {
  allo[[v]] = factor(allo[[v]], levels = c("no", "yes"))
}
allo$density_100 = (allo$density_ha - 1200) / 100

# Colours (Okabe-Ito) of the four sites; filled symbols for shaded trees.
site_colours = c(CIV1 = "#E69F00", CIV2 = "#56B4E9", ECU = "#009E73", NGA = "#CC79A7")
shade_symbols = c(no = 1, yes = 19)

# Formatting of numbers quoted in the text.
f0 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0)
f1 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
```

# Exploratory data analysis {#sec-eda}

## The fields and their management {#sec-design}

One row per field, with the number of trees, the range of diameters and the management:

```{r}
fields = data.frame(
  site = tapply(as.character(allo$site), allo$field, unique),
  age = tapply(allo$age_years, allo$field, unique),
  trees = as.vector(table(allo$field)),
  dia_min = tapply(allo$dia20_cm, allo$field, min),
  dia_max = tapply(allo$dia20_cm, allo$field, max),
  shade = tapply(as.character(allo$shade), allo$field, unique),
  density = tapply(allo$density_ha, allo$field, unique),
  irrigation = tapply(as.character(allo$irrigation), allo$field, unique),
  fertilised = tapply(allo$fertilisation == "yes", allo$field, sum)
)
fields
```

There are `r nrow(allo)` trees in `r nlevels(allo$field)` fields, with 3 to
`r max(fields$trees)` trees per field. Every management variable except fertilisation is
a property of the field, and almost every one is a property of the site:

- **irrigation** is "yes" exactly at CIV2 and ECU;
- **shade** is "yes" at CIV2, NGA and in the oldest CIV1 field (CIV1_19, 3 trees), the
  only contrast within a site;
- **planting density** is `r paste(sort(unique(fields$density)), collapse = ", ")`
  trees/ha; it is constant within CIV1, CIV2 and NGA, and within ECU the 11-year field has
  1,130 and the younger fields 1,500 trees/ha, a contrast confounded with age;
- **fertilisation** is "no" at CIV1 and "yes" at CIV2 and ECU, and in each NGA field 3 of
  the 6 trees were fertilised: the only contrast within a field.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: management is a property of the site"}
With four sites, a variable that takes one value per site is the site under another name.
The shaded trees are those of CIV2 and NGA (plus one CIV1 field), the unshaded those of
ECU and the younger CIV1 fields; a "shade effect" estimated from these data is a
difference between countries, planting material, climate, collectors and years as much as
between shaded and unshaded trees. Only three contrasts lie within a site: shade in CIV1
(one field of 3 trees against three fields), density in ECU (one field, which is also the
oldest) and fertilisation in NGA (within fields). @sec-candidates fits the site itself as
a candidate.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the field descriptions do not agree everywhere"}
Table 1 of the manuscript describes the CIV1 field of 1.5 years as intercropped with
plantain and shaded, but the spreadsheet gives shade "no" for its trees (@sec-sensitivity
fits both). The two CIV2 fields (2 and 3.25 years) have the same GPS position in Table 1
and were sampled in 2019 and 2020, so they may be the same plantation sampled twice;
Table 1 gives the second age as 3 years. The wood density (0.39 g/cm³) is the same value
from the literature for every tree, so the term $\log(\mathrm{WD})$ of the manuscript's
equations is part of the intercept.
:::

## Biomass against diameter {#sec-scatter}

@fig-scatter shows the aboveground biomass against the diameter on the original and on
logarithmic axes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Aboveground biomass against stem diameter at 20 cm, on the original scale
#|   (left) and on logarithmic axes (right). Colours mark the sites; filled symbols are
#|   shaded trees. The three labelled trees are discussed in the text."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
flagged = allo$tree %in% c("F9", "D4", "D5")
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(agb_kg ~ dia20_cm, data = allo, col = site_colours[as.character(allo$site)],
     pch = shade_symbols[as.character(allo$shade)],
     xlab = "Stem diameter at 20 cm (cm)", ylab = "Aboveground biomass (kg)")
# Label only F9 here; D4 and D5 overlap on this scale.
text(allo$dia20_cm[allo$tree == "F9"], allo$agb_kg[allo$tree == "F9"], "F9", pos = 3,
     cex = 0.7)
legend("topleft", legend = names(site_colours), col = site_colours, pch = 15, bty = "n")
plot(agb_kg ~ dia20_cm, data = allo, log = "xy",
     col = site_colours[as.character(allo$site)],
     pch = shade_symbols[as.character(allo$shade)],
     xlab = "Stem diameter at 20 cm (cm)", ylab = "Aboveground biomass (kg)")
text(allo$dia20_cm[flagged], allo$agb_kg[flagged], allo$tree[flagged], pos = 4,
     cex = 0.7)
legend("topleft", legend = c("unshaded", "shaded"), pch = shade_symbols, bty = "n")
par(old_par)
```

On logarithmic axes the trees lie close to a straight line over two orders of magnitude of
diameter and three of biomass, which is what a power law predicts (@sec-model). On the
original scale the spread of the biomass grows with the diameter. Three trees stand apart:
F9 (CIV1, 37 cm) has far less biomass than any tree of similar diameter, and the two
smallest trees, D4 and D5 (ECU, 1 year), have as much biomass as trees twice their
diameter. The young trees of each site form clusters, and the shaded trees (filled) leave
a gap between the CIV2 trees, up to about 9 cm, and the NGA and CIV1_19 trees, from about
15 cm.

## Implausible records {#sec-records}

A simple check of plausibility compares the wood mass of a tree with the mass of a
cylinder with the diameter of its stem and the height of the tree, made of wood of density
0.39 g/cm³ (the value used in the manuscript):

$$
F = \frac{W}{\rho\,\frac{\pi}{4}\,D^2\,H},
$$

where $W$ is the dry mass of the wood (g), $\rho = 0.39$ g/cm³, $D$ the diameter (cm) and
$H$ the height (cm). The stem tapers, so $F$ (a form factor) is usually below 1; branches
add wood, so a bushy tree can exceed 1, but not by a factor of ten.

```{r}
cylinder_kg = 0.39 * pi / 4 * allo$dia20_cm^2 * (100 * allo$height_m) / 1000
allo$form_factor = allo$wood_kg / cylinder_kg
form_order = order(allo$form_factor)
show_cols = c("tree", "field", "dia20_cm", "height_m", "wood_kg", "agb_kg", "form_factor")
knitr::kable(allo[form_order[c(1:3, (nrow(allo) - 3):nrow(allo))], show_cols],
             digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
ff = setNames(allo$form_factor, allo$tree)
ff_others = ff[!names(ff) %in% c("F9", "D4", "D5")]
ecu_young = ff[allo$site == "ECU" & allo$age_years < 10 &
                 !names(ff) %in% c("D4", "D5", "D10")]
ecu_11 = ff[allo$field == "ECU_11" & names(ff) != "D14"]
```

All trees but three have a form factor between `r f2(min(ff_others))` and
`r f2(max(ff_others))`; the young, hedged and bushy ECU trees of 1 and 6 years have most of
the highest values (`r f2(min(ecu_young))` to `r f2(max(ecu_young))`, without D4, D5 and
D10). F9 has `r f2(ff[["F9"]])`, and D4 and
D5 have `r f1(ff[["D4"]])` and `r f1(ff[["D5"]])`. The manuscript excluded F9 as an
outlier ("probably because of dieback or an unreported management intervention"), but
calls it "the oldest tree" of Côte d'Ivoire, whereas it is 10 years old and the CIV1_19
trees are older. For D4 and D5, a diameter of about 0.7 cm with 0.16 to 0.17 kg of wood
would need a wood density of several g/cm³; a typing error in the diameter (or in the
mass) is more likely than such trees. We exclude all three from the main analysis: the
main data set has `r nrow(allo) - 3` trees. @sec-sensitivity repeats the analysis with the
`r nrow(allo) - 1` trees of the manuscript (only F9 excluded).

```{r}
main = allo[!allo$tree %in% c("F9", "D4", "D5"), ]
main = droplevels(main)
rownames(main) = NULL
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: other records that do not add up"}
These do not justify an exclusion but should be known:

- **T17** (CIV2, 3.25 years) has `r allo$agb_kg[allo$tree == "T17"]` kg of aboveground
  biomass, but its wood and leaves sum to
  `r allo$wood_kg[allo$tree == "T17"] + allo$leaf_kg[allo$tree == "T17"]` kg; every other
  tree adds up. We use the recorded AGB.
- **F11 and F12** (CIV1_19) have the same wood mass
  (`r allo$wood_kg[allo$tree == "F11"]` kg) with diameters of
  `r allo$dia20_cm[allo$tree == "F11"]` and `r allo$dia20_cm[allo$tree == "F12"]` cm,
  perhaps a copied value.
- **D10 and D14** (ECU) look as if their diameters were swapped. D10 (6 years,
  `r allo$dia20_cm[allo$tree == "D10"]` cm, `r f1(allo$agb_kg[allo$tree == "D10"])` kg) is
  the thickest tree of its field with less biomass than a tree of 8.6 cm, and D14 (11
  years, `r allo$dia20_cm[allo$tree == "D14"]` cm, `r f1(allo$agb_kg[allo$tree == "D14"])`
  kg) the thinnest of its field with as much biomass as trees of 15 to 17 cm. Their form
  factors (`r f2(ff[["D10"]])` and `r f2(ff[["D14"]])`) are the lowest and the highest of
  the ECU trees of 6 and 11 years (the other trees of the 11-year field have
  `r f2(min(ecu_11))` to `r f2(max(ecu_11))`). With the two diameters exchanged, each tree
  fits its field. This cannot be verified from the data, so it is a sensitivity
  check (@sec-sensitivity) and not a correction.
:::

## What we take forward

- **The curve:** a power law of the diameter (a straight line on logarithmic axes).
- **The observations:** positive biomasses whose spread grows with the mean, so a
  LogNormal or Gamma distribution rather than a Normal one with constant variance.
- **The groups:** trees of one field share age, planting material, management, collector
  and year of sampling, so they are not independent; a random effect per field.
- **The predictors:** shade, density, irrigation and fertilisation, and the site, as fixed
  effects on the parameters of the power law through model matrices (Chapter 7,
  `sec-model-matrix`).

# The model {#sec-model}

## The power law

The mean aboveground biomass of a tree with diameter $D$ (cm) is described by a power law
(functions supplement, `sec-fn-power`), written with a reference diameter of 10 cm:

$$
\mu(D) = a\left(\frac{D}{10}\right)^{b},
$$

where $b$ is the allometric exponent (no units: an increase of 1% in the diameter
increases the mean biomass by about $b$%) and $a$ is the mean biomass (kg) of a tree with
a diameter of 10 cm. This is the form $y_0(x/x_0)^b$ of the supplement, so here $a$ is
the value at 10 cm and not at 1 cm. The reference makes $a$ interpretable and inside the
data, and it makes the estimates of $\log(a)$ and $b$ much less correlated than with the
reference 1 cm, which is far below most trees. For a cylinder of constant shape and wood
density, biomass grows with $D^3$; for a cylinder of constant height with $D^2$.

On logarithmic axes the power law is a straight line, $\log(\mu) = \log(a) + b\log(D/10)$.
The manuscript fitted this line (its equation 1) and cubic polynomials of $\log(D)$ to
$\log(\mathrm{AGB})$ with Normal errors. A line fitted to the logarithm of the biomass
describes the median and not the mean: if $\log(Y)$ is Normal with mean $m$ and standard
deviation $\sigma$, $Y$ is LogNormal with median $e^{m}$ and mean $e^{m + \sigma^2/2}$. The
"correction factor" $e^{\sigma^2/2}$ of the manuscript (Clifford et al. 2013) converts the
median into the mean. We write the LogNormal distribution with its mean $\mu$ instead
(`meanlog = log(mu) - sdlog^2 / 2`, as in the infiltration analysis), so that the curve is
the mean and needs no correction.

## The model for the trees

For tree $i$ in field $j$, with aboveground biomass $Y_{ij}$ (kg) and diameter $D_{ij}$
(cm), the model with shade on both parameters of the power law is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_j &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{field}}),\\
\log(a_j) &= \beta_{a,0} + \beta_{a,\mathrm{shade}}\,S_j + u_j,\\
b_j &= \beta_{b,0} + \beta_{b,\mathrm{shade}}\,S_j,\\
\mu_{ij} &= a_j\left(\frac{D_{ij}}{10}\right)^{b_j},\\
\log(Y_{ij}) \mid u_j &\sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(\log(\mu_{ij}) - \sigma^2/2,\ \sigma^2\right),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $S_j$ is 1 if field $j$ is shaded and 0 otherwise, $\sigma$ is the standard
deviation of $\log(Y_{ij})$ among trees of one field with the same diameter, and the trees
are independent for given $u_j$. The last line says that $Y_{ij}$ is LogNormal with mean
$\mu_{ij}$. The deviation $u_j$ of a field multiplies the mean biomass of all its trees by
$e^{u_j}$, whatever their diameter. Other candidates replace $S_j$ by other predictors, or
let them change only $\log(a)$ (@sec-candidates).

The answer is the typical mean biomass ($u_j = 0$) of shaded and of unshaded trees with
diameters of 4 and 16 cm, and the ratio shaded/unshaded at each diameter. With $u_j = 0$,
the curve is that of the median field; the mean over fields is $e^{\sigma^2_{\mathrm{field}}/2}$
times higher.

## Implementation

One joint NLL covers every model of this document. Three choices are elements of the list
of data:

- `distribution`: `"LogNormal"`, `"Gamma"` (mean $\mu$ and shape $k$), `"Normal"` (constant
  standard deviation) or `"NormalPower"` (standard deviation $\sigma\mu^{\delta}$, so that the
  variance is a power of the mean);
- `random`: the grouping of the random effect, `"field"`, `"site"` or `"none"`;
- `degree`: 1 for the power law; 2 or 3 add the terms $c_2\log(D/10)^2$ and
  $c_3\log(D/10)^3$ to $\log(\mu)$, the quadratic and cubic polynomials of the manuscript
  (its equations 2 and 5).

The predictors enter through the model matrices `X_a` and `X_b`. Fertilisation varies
within NGA fields, so the matrices have one row per tree (and not one per field). Two more
matrices, `X_a_answer` and `X_b_answer`, come from a data frame with one row per
combination of predictor and diameter of the answer (`answer_dia`), and `ADREPORT()` gives
the logarithm of the typical mean there (`log_mu_answer`) and, through the matrix
`answer_contrast`, differences of these logarithms (`log_ratio`).

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)
```

```{r}
allo_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  agb = OBS(agb)
  nll = 0
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the groups, before they are used.
  if (random != "none") {
    nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_group), log = TRUE))
  }
  # Logarithm of the mean biomass of each tree.
  log_dia = log(dia / 10)
  log_a = X_a %*% beta_a
  if (random != "none") {
    log_a = log_a + u[group]
  }
  log_mu = log_a + (X_b %*% beta_b) * log_dia
  # Typical mean biomass (u = 0) at the combinations of the answer.
  log_dia_answer = log(answer_dia / 10)
  log_mu_answer = X_a_answer %*% beta_a + (X_b_answer %*% beta_b) * log_dia_answer
  # Polynomial terms of the manuscript's equations.
  if (degree > 1) {
    for (k in 2:degree) {
      log_mu = log_mu + beta_poly[k - 1] * log_dia^k
      log_mu_answer = log_mu_answer + beta_poly[k - 1] * log_dia_answer^k
    }
  }
  ADREPORT(log_mu_answer)
  if (nrow(answer_contrast) > 0) {
    log_ratio = answer_contrast %*% log_mu_answer
    ADREPORT(log_ratio)
  }
  mu = exp(log_mu)
  # Minus the log density of the biomasses for given deviations.
  if (distribution == "LogNormal") {
    sdlog = exp(log_disp)
    nll = nll - sum(dlnorm(x = agb, meanlog = log(mu) - sdlog^2 / 2, sdlog = sdlog,
                           log = TRUE))
  } else if (distribution == "Gamma") {
    shape = exp(log_disp)
    nll = nll - sum(dgamma(x = agb, shape = shape, scale = mu / shape, log = TRUE))
  } else if (distribution == "Normal") {
    nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = agb, mean = mu, sd = exp(log_disp), log = TRUE))
  } else {
    nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = agb, mean = mu, sd = exp(log_disp) * mu^power,
                          log = TRUE))
  }
  nll
}
```

`allo_setup()` builds the list of data and the starting values for a data frame of trees,
a list of formulas (for $\log(a)$ and $b$), the three choices above and, optionally, the
data frame and contrast matrix of the answer. The baseline starting values are
$a = 10$ kg (a tree of 10 cm in @fig-scatter) and $b = 2$; every effect starts at zero.

```{r}
allo_setup = function(trees, formulas = list(a = ~ 1, b = ~ 1),
                      distribution = "LogNormal", random = "field", degree = 1,
                      answer_info = trees[1, ], answer_contrast = NULL) {
  data = list(agb = trees$agb_kg, dia = trees$dia20_cm, distribution = distribution,
              random = random, degree = degree,
              X_a = model.matrix(formulas$a, data = trees),
              X_b = model.matrix(formulas$b, data = trees),
              X_a_answer = model.matrix(formulas$a, data = answer_info),
              X_b_answer = model.matrix(formulas$b, data = answer_info),
              answer_dia = answer_info$dia20_cm)
  if (is.null(answer_contrast)) {
    answer_contrast = matrix(0, nrow = 0, ncol = nrow(answer_info))
  }
  data$answer_contrast = answer_contrast
  start = list(beta_a = c(log(10), rep(0, ncol(data$X_a) - 1)),
               beta_b = c(2, rep(0, ncol(data$X_b) - 1)))
  if (degree > 1) {
    start$beta_poly = rep(0, degree - 1)
  }
  start$log_disp = switch(distribution, LogNormal = log(0.3), Gamma = log(10),
                          Normal = log(5), NormalPower = log(0.3))
  if (distribution == "NormalPower") {
    start$power = 1
  }
  if (random != "none") {
    data$group = as.numeric(droplevels(trees[[random]]))
    start$log_sd_group = log(0.3)
    start$u = rep(0, max(data$group))
  }
  list(data = data, start = start)
}
```

`fit_allo()` processes the joint NLL, integrating out `u` when the model has a random
effect, and minimises it. For several models of @sec-candidates the likelihood has two
maxima, one with a small and one with a large variation among fields (@sec-two-maxima), so
`fit_allo()` starts the standard deviation among groups at three values (0.05, 0.3 and 1),
keeps the fit with the lowest NLL and records the difference between the highest and the
lowest NLL that the three starts reached (`nll_gap`, zero when they agree). Chapter 8
draws such starting values at random; three fixed values keep this document
deterministic. With `reml = TRUE`, the fixed effects are integrated out as well (REML,
Chapter 7).

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

fit_allo = function(setup, nll = allo_nll, sd_starts = c(0.05, 0.3, 1), reml = FALSE) {
  random = NULL
  if (setup$data$random != "none") {
    random = "u"
  } else {
    sd_starts = NA
  }
  if (reml) {
    random = c(random, grep("^beta", names(setup$start), value = TRUE))
  }
  best = NULL
  values = c()
  for (s in sd_starts) {
    start = setup$start
    if (!is.na(s)) {
      start$log_sd_group = log(s)
    }
    obj = MakeADFun(cmb(nll, setup$data), start, random = random, silent = TRUE)
    fit = optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
    values = c(values, fit$value)
    if (is.null(best) || fit$value < best$fit$value) {
      best = list(obj = obj, fit = fit)
    }
  }
  best$nll_gap = max(values) - min(values)
  best
}
```

Three helpers complete the toolkit:

- `aic_table()` reports, for a named list of fits, $K$, the log-likelihood, the
  convergence code, the largest absolute gradient at the solution, `nll_gap`, the
  standard deviation among groups, AIC and the difference from the lowest AIC;
- `allo_answer()` gives the typical mean biomass at the combinations of the answer, and
  `allo_ratio()` the ratios, with Wald intervals calculated on the log scale and
  transformed back;
- `show_table()` prints a table in the document.

```{r}
aic_table = function(fits) {
  out = data.frame(
    model = names(fits),
    K = sapply(fits, function(f) length(f$fit$par)),
    loglik = sapply(fits, function(f) -f$fit$value),
    convergence = sapply(fits, function(f) f$fit$convergence),
    max_gradient = sapply(fits, function(f) max(abs(f$obj$gr(f$fit$par)))),
    nll_gap = sapply(fits, function(f) f$nll_gap),
    sd_group = sapply(fits, function(f) {
      if ("log_sd_group" %in% names(f$fit$par)) exp(f$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]]) else NA
    })
  )
  out$aic = 2 * out$K - 2 * out$loglik
  out$delta_aic = out$aic - min(out$aic)
  rownames(out) = NULL
  out
}

critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
report_rows = function(fit, name) {
  report = summary(sdreport(fit$obj), select = "report")
  report[rownames(report) == name, , drop = FALSE]
}
allo_answer = function(fit, answer_info) {
  r = report_rows(fit, "log_mu_answer")
  out = answer_info
  out$agb_kg = exp(r[, "Estimate"])
  out$lower = exp(r[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * r[, "Std. Error"])
  out$upper = exp(r[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * r[, "Std. Error"])
  rownames(out) = NULL
  out
}
allo_ratio = function(fit, dia) {
  r = report_rows(fit, "log_ratio")
  data.frame(dia20_cm = dia, ratio = exp(r[, "Estimate"]),
             lower = exp(r[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * r[, "Std. Error"]),
             upper = exp(r[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * r[, "Std. Error"]))
}

# Print an AIC table or an answer table in the document.
show_table = function(tab, digits = 2) {
  for (col in intersect(c("max_gradient", "nll_gap"), names(tab))) {
    tab[[col]] = format(signif(tab[[col]], 2))
  }
  knitr::kable(tab, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
}
```

# Which curve, distribution and random effect? {#sec-choices}

We compare, for the power law without predictors, four distributions with a random effect
per field, the LogNormal distribution with a random effect per site and without a random
effect, and the quadratic and cubic polynomials of $\log(D/10)$ with the LogNormal
distribution and a random effect per field.

```{r}
choices = data.frame(
  distribution = c("LogNormal", "Gamma", "Normal", "NormalPower", "LogNormal",
                   "LogNormal", "LogNormal", "LogNormal"),
  random = c("field", "field", "field", "field", "site", "none", "field", "field"),
  degree = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3)
)
choice_fits = list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(choices))) {
  setup = allo_setup(main, distribution = choices$distribution[i],
                     random = choices$random[i], degree = choices$degree[i])
  choice_fits[[i]] = fit_allo(setup)
}
names(choice_fits) = paste(choices$distribution, choices$random,
                           c("power", "quadratic", "cubic")[choices$degree])
choice_table = aic_table(choice_fits)
show_table(choice_table, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
delta_choice = setNames(choice_table$delta_aic, choice_table$model)
aic_choice = setNames(choice_table$aic, choice_table$model)
power_fit = choice_fits[[1]]
power_par = power_fit$fit$par
sigma_power = exp(power_par[["log_disp"]])
sd_field_power = exp(power_par[["log_sd_group"]])
power_sd = summary(sdreport(power_fit$obj), select = "fixed")
```

`r if (all(choice_table$convergence == 0)) "All eight fits converged" else "Not every fit converged (see the table)"`,
and the three starting values of the standard deviation among groups reached the same
maximum in every fit (`nll_gap` below
`r if (max(choice_table$nll_gap) < 0.001) "0.001" else f2(max(choice_table$nll_gap))`). The LogNormal and Gamma distributions are
within `r f1(abs(aic_choice[["LogNormal field power"]] - aic_choice[["Gamma field power"]]))` AIC
units of each other, and the Normal distribution with a variance that is a power of the
mean is as good (its power $\delta$ is estimated at
`r f2(choice_fits[[4]]$fit$par[["power"]])`, so the standard deviation is almost
proportional to the mean, as in the LogNormal and Gamma distributions). The Normal
distribution with constant variance is
`r f0(aic_choice[["Normal field power"]] - aic_choice[["LogNormal field power"]])` AIC units worse
than the LogNormal. We use the LogNormal distribution, which is the model behind the
log-log regressions of the allometric literature. Its standard deviation of
$\log(Y_{ij})$ is $\sigma =$ `r f2(sigma_power)`, so the manuscript's correction factor
would be $e^{\sigma^2/2} =$ `r f2(exp(sigma_power^2 / 2))`.

A random effect per field is better than one per site
(`r f1(aic_choice[["LogNormal site power"]] - aic_choice[["LogNormal field power"]])` AIC units) and
than none (`r f1(aic_choice[["LogNormal none power"]] - aic_choice[["LogNormal field power"]])`
units). The standard deviation among fields is `r f2(sd_field_power)` on the log scale:
the mean biomass of the trees of a typical field lies within a factor of about
`r f1(exp(2 * sd_field_power))` above or below the typical curve. Trees of one field share
their age, planting material, management, collector and year of sampling, so they deviate
from the curve together; a site has fields of different ages and its random effect cannot
describe that. With only four levels, a random effect per site would also be poorly
estimated.

The quadratic and cubic polynomials improve the log-likelihood by
`r f1(choice_table$loglik[7] - choice_table$loglik[1])` and
`r f1(choice_table$loglik[8] - choice_table$loglik[1])` units for one and two parameters
more, and their AIC is within `r f1(max(abs(choice_table$aic[7:8] - choice_table$aic[1])))`
units of that of the power law. On these `r nrow(main)` trees, the data give no clear
reason to bend the straight line on logarithmic axes. The estimates of the power law:

```{r}
round(power_sd, 3)
```

The exponent is `r f2(power_par[["beta_b"]])` (standard error
`r f2(power_sd["beta_b", "Std. Error"])`), and a tree of 10 cm has a typical mean biomass
of `r f1(exp(power_par[["beta_a"]]))` kg.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: a Normal distribution with constant variance"}
The biomass of the trees ranges from `r min(main$agb_kg)` to `r max(main$agb_kg)` kg, and
the spread among trees of similar diameter grows with their size (@fig-scatter). A Normal
distribution with constant variance gives the large trees almost all the weight and
treats a deviation of 1 kg in a tree of 0.2 kg like one in a tree of 80 kg. The
manuscript avoids this by fitting the logarithm of the biomass; a non-linear model fitted
on the original scale must choose a distribution whose variance grows with the mean.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative: nested random effects (beyond Chapter 7)"}
Fields are nested in sites, so a model could have a deviation $v_s$ per site and a
deviation $u_j$ per field. A short NLL with both:

```{r}
allo_nll_2re = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  agb = OBS(agb)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_group), log = TRUE))
  nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = v, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_site), log = TRUE))
  mu = exp(beta_a + u[group] + v[site_index] + beta_b * log(dia / 10))
  sdlog = exp(log_disp)
  nll - sum(dlnorm(x = agb, meanlog = log(mu) - sdlog^2 / 2, sdlog = sdlog, log = TRUE))
}
setup_2re = allo_setup(main)
setup_2re$data$site_index = as.numeric(main$site)
setup_2re$start$log_sd_site = log(0.3)
setup_2re$start$v = rep(0, nlevels(main$site))
obj_2re = MakeADFun(cmb(allo_nll_2re, setup_2re$data), setup_2re$start,
                    random = c("u", "v"), silent = TRUE)
fit_2re = optim(par = obj_2re$par, fn = obj_2re$fn, gr = obj_2re$gr, method = "BFGS")
c(convergence = fit_2re$convergence,
  delta_aic = (2 * length(fit_2re$par) + 2 * fit_2re$value) - aic_choice[[1]],
  exp(fit_2re$par[c("log_sd_group", "log_sd_site")]))
```

The second random effect does not improve AIC (the difference is
`r f2((2 * length(fit_2re$par) + 2 * fit_2re$value) - aic_choice[[1]])` units): the
variation is split between sites (standard deviation
`r f2(exp(fit_2re$par[["log_sd_site"]]))`) and fields within sites
(`r f2(exp(fit_2re$par[["log_sd_group"]]))`), and four sites cannot tell the two apart
well.
:::

## The cubic polynomial of the manuscript {#sec-cubic}

The manuscript selected its equation 5, a cubic polynomial of $\log(D)$, as the best
base equation, with a large lead over the power law (its Table 5). On the
`r nrow(main)` trees of the main data set, the cubic is no better than the power law. On
the `r nrow(allo) - 1` trees of the manuscript (with D4 and D5):

```{r}
manuscript_trees = droplevels(allo[allo$tree != "F9", ])
cubic_compare = list(
  power = fit_allo(allo_setup(manuscript_trees)),
  quadratic = fit_allo(allo_setup(manuscript_trees, degree = 2)),
  cubic = fit_allo(allo_setup(manuscript_trees, degree = 3))
)
cubic_table = aic_table(cubic_compare)
show_table(cubic_table, digits = 1)
```

Now the cubic is `r f1(cubic_table$aic[1] - cubic_table$aic[3])` AIC units better than the
power law: the curvature comes from the two small trees D4 and D5, which are much heavier
than the line through the other small trees predicts. The slope of the cubic on
logarithmic axes, $b + 2c_2\log(D/10) + 3c_3\log(D/10)^2$, is zero where the curve turns:

```{r}
cubic_par = cubic_compare$cubic$fit$par
cubic_b = cubic_par[["beta_b"]]
cubic_poly = cubic_par[names(cubic_par) == "beta_poly"]
# Roots of the slope, a quadratic polynomial of log(D / 10).
turning_log = Re(polyroot(c(cubic_b, 2 * cubic_poly[1], 3 * cubic_poly[2])))
turning_dia = sort(10 * exp(turning_log))
turning_dia
range(manuscript_trees$dia20_cm)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
main_cubic = choice_fits[[8]]$fit$par
main_turning = sort(10 * exp(Re(polyroot(c(main_cubic[["beta_b"]],
  2 * main_cubic[names(main_cubic) == "beta_poly"][1],
  3 * main_cubic[names(main_cubic) == "beta_poly"][2])))))
```

The fitted cubic has a minimum at `r f1(turning_dia[1])` cm, inside the range of the
data (below it the biomass rises as the diameter falls, to pass through D4 and D5), and a
maximum at `r f1(turning_dia[2])` cm, just above the largest tree: beyond it, thicker trees
would have less biomass. On the main data set the turning points lie at
`r f1(main_turning[1])` and `r f1(main_turning[2])` cm, outside the data.

@fig-cubic shows both fits.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cubic
#| fig-cap: "The cubic polynomial of log(D/10) (solid) and the power law (dashed), typical
#|   curves (u = 0) fitted to the 61 trees of the manuscript, on logarithmic axes (left)
#|   and on the original scale up to 45 cm (right). D4 and D5 are the two open circles
#|   at the lower left."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
typical_curve = function(par, dia) {
  log_dia = log(dia / 10)
  out = par[["beta_a"]] + par[["beta_b"]] * log_dia
  poly = par[names(par) == "beta_poly"]
  for (k in seq_along(poly)) {
    out = out + poly[k] * log_dia^(k + 1)
  }
  exp(out)
}
dia_grid = exp(seq(from = log(0.5), to = log(45), length.out = 200))
power_61 = cubic_compare$power$fit$par
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(agb_kg ~ dia20_cm, data = manuscript_trees, log = "xy",
     pch = ifelse(manuscript_trees$tree %in% c("D4", "D5"), 1, 19), col = "grey40",
     xlab = "Stem diameter at 20 cm (cm)", ylab = "Aboveground biomass (kg)")
lines(dia_grid, typical_curve(cubic_par, dia_grid), lwd = 2)
lines(dia_grid, typical_curve(power_61, dia_grid), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
plot(agb_kg ~ dia20_cm, data = manuscript_trees, xlim = c(0, 45), ylim = c(0, 140),
     pch = 19, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "Stem diameter at 20 cm (cm)", ylab = "Aboveground biomass (kg)")
lines(dia_grid, typical_curve(cubic_par, dia_grid), lwd = 2)
lines(dia_grid, typical_curve(power_61, dia_grid), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
par(old_par)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: a cubic polynomial on logarithmic axes"}
A polynomial of $\log(D)$ is flexible but not monotonic: it can make biomass fall as the
diameter grows, which no tree does. In the manuscript's Figure 3, the base model turns (according to its text) at
about 35 cm, and the curves for high planting density (with and without shade) reach a
maximum at about 25 cm and then fall, inside the range of the data. The curvature that
the cubic captures comes from a few records (D4 and D5 here), and the extra parameters
describe them rather than the trees in general. A power law cannot turn; if the data
called for a bend, a monotonic curve with a bend (a power law whose exponent changes
smoothly, or a saturating function) would be the non-linear alternative (Picard et al.
2015 discuss alternatives to the power law).
:::

# Does management change the allometry? {#sec-candidates}

With the LogNormal distribution and a random effect per field, the candidates differ in
the predictors of $\log(a)$ and $b$:

- `none`: one power law for all trees;
- `shade`, `density`, `irrigation`, `fertilisation`: the predictor changes $\log(a)$ only
  (curves parallel on logarithmic axes);
- `shade_b`, `density_b`, `irrigation_b`: the predictor changes $\log(a)$ and $b$;
- `shade_density_b`: shade and density both change $\log(a)$ and $b$ (the closest to the
  manuscript's final model);
- `site`, `site_b`: the site changes $\log(a)$, or $\log(a)$ and $b$;
- `site_fert`: as `site_b`, with fertilisation on $\log(a)$; given the site, its effect is
  the contrast within the NGA fields;
- `site_shade_density`: as `site_b`, with shade and density on $\log(a)$; given the site,
  their effects come from the contrasts within CIV1 and ECU.

The manuscript's interaction between density and the cross-sectional area of the stem
(proportional to $D^2$) lets the effect of density change with the size of the tree, which
is what density on $b$ does here.

```{r}
candidates = list(
  none = list(a = ~ 1, b = ~ 1),
  shade = list(a = ~ shade, b = ~ 1),
  density = list(a = ~ density_100, b = ~ 1),
  irrigation = list(a = ~ irrigation, b = ~ 1),
  fertilisation = list(a = ~ fertilisation, b = ~ 1),
  shade_b = list(a = ~ shade, b = ~ shade),
  density_b = list(a = ~ density_100, b = ~ density_100),
  irrigation_b = list(a = ~ irrigation, b = ~ irrigation),
  shade_density_b = list(a = ~ shade + density_100, b = ~ shade + density_100),
  site = list(a = ~ site, b = ~ 1),
  site_b = list(a = ~ site, b = ~ site),
  site_fert = list(a = ~ site + fertilisation, b = ~ site),
  site_shade_density = list(a = ~ site + shade + density_100, b = ~ site)
)
fit_candidates = function(trees, candidates) {
  fits = list()
  for (m in names(candidates)) {
    fits[[m]] = fit_allo(allo_setup(trees, formulas = candidates[[m]]))
  }
  fits
}
candidate_fits = fit_candidates(main, candidates)
candidate_table = aic_table(candidate_fits)
show_table(candidate_table, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
delta_cand = setNames(candidate_table$delta_aic, candidate_table$model)
aic_cand = setNames(candidate_table$aic, candidate_table$model)
gap_cand = setNames(candidate_table$nll_gap, candidate_table$model)
sd_cand = setNames(candidate_table$sd_group, candidate_table$model)
best_mgmt = c("shade_b", "density_b", "shade_density_b")[
  which.min(aic_cand[c("shade_b", "density_b", "shade_density_b")])]
```

`r if (all(candidate_table$convergence == 0)) "All fits converged" else "Not every fit converged (see the table)"`
(largest absolute gradient `r f2(max(candidate_table$max_gradient))`). A management
variable on $\log(a)$ alone helps little: density lowers AIC by
`r f1(aic_cand[["none"]] - aic_cand[["density"]])` units and irrigation by
`r f1(aic_cand[["none"]] - aic_cand[["irrigation"]])`, while shade and fertilisation change
it by `r f1(aic_cand[["shade"]] - aic_cand[["none"]])` and
`r f1(aic_cand[["fertilisation"]] - aic_cand[["none"]])` units. On both parameters, shade and
density help a lot (`shade_b` is `r f1(aic_cand[["none"]] - aic_cand[["shade_b"]])` and
`density_b` `r f1(aic_cand[["none"]] - aic_cand[["density_b"]])` units better than `none`),
irrigation does not. But the site on both parameters (`site_b`) is better still:
`r f1(aic_cand[[best_mgmt]] - aic_cand[["site_b"]])` units better than the best model
with management only (`r best_mgmt`). Adding fertilisation to `site_b` changes AIC by
`r f1(aic_cand[["site_fert"]] - aic_cand[["site_b"]])` units, and shade with density
by `r f1(aic_cand[["site_shade_density"]] - aic_cand[["site_b"]])`.

The effects of management given the site, from the within-site contrasts, on the log scale
of $a$:

```{r}
within_site = rbind(
  fertilisation = summary(sdreport(candidate_fits$site_fert$obj),
                          select = "fixed")[5, ],
  shade = summary(sdreport(candidate_fits$site_shade_density$obj),
                  select = "fixed")[5, ],
  density_100 = summary(sdreport(candidate_fits$site_shade_density$obj),
                        select = "fixed")[6, ]
)
round(within_site, 3)
```

Fertilisation within NGA multiplies the mean biomass by
`r f2(exp(within_site["fertilisation", 1]))` (95% Wald interval
`r f2(exp(within_site["fertilisation", 1] - critical_value * within_site["fertilisation", 2]))`
to
`r f2(exp(within_site["fertilisation", 1] + critical_value * within_site["fertilisation", 2]))`):
no effect is detectable. The shade effect within CIV1 rests on one field of 3 trees and
has a standard error (`r f2(within_site["shade", 2])`) larger than the effect
(`r f2(within_site["shade", 1])`). The density effect within ECU
(`r f2(within_site["density_100", 1])` per 100 trees/ha, standard error
`r f2(within_site["density_100", 2])`) rests on one field with fewer trees per hectare that
is also the oldest, and it has the sign opposite to the manuscript's (here less biomass at
higher density). These are the only estimates of management in these data that are not
differences between sites, and none of them can be separated from age or from a single
field.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the site explains more than any management variable"}
Each management variable on $\log(a)$ and $b$ splits the 12 fields into two or three
groups of sites. The site on both parameters fits better than any such split, so the data
prefer differences among sites that no management variable describes. When a management
variable improves the fit over `none`, the improvement is evidence that sites differ, not
that the variable is the reason. The manuscript compared models with and without
management, but never with the site (`dataset`) as a fixed effect, which was its random
effect; with four levels the variance among sites is poorly estimated, and the fixed
management effects take over the differences among sites.
:::

## Two maxima of the likelihood {#sec-two-maxima}

For several candidates the three starting values reach different maxima (`nll_gap` above
0.05 in the table): `r paste0("\x60", names(gap_cand)[gap_cand > 0.05], "\x60", collapse = ", ")`.
Gaps of about 0.01 are fits that stop at slightly different points near a standard
deviation of zero, where the likelihood is flat. The two fits of `shade_b` from a small
and from a large starting value:

```{r}
shade_setup = allo_setup(main, formulas = candidates$shade_b)
shade_small = fit_allo(shade_setup, sd_starts = 0.05)
shade_large = fit_allo(shade_setup, sd_starts = 1)
shade_modes = rbind(small = c(shade_small$fit$par, nll = shade_small$fit$value),
                    large = c(shade_large$fit$par, nll = shade_large$fit$value))
colnames(shade_modes) = c("log_a", "log_a_shade", "b", "b_shade", "log_sigma",
                          "log_sd_field", "nll")
round(shade_modes, 3)
```

With a small standard deviation among fields (`r f2(exp(shade_modes["small", "log_sd_field"]))`),
the exponents come from the whole range of diameters, across fields: about
`r f1(shade_modes["small", "b"])` for unshaded and
`r f1(shade_modes["small", "b"] + shade_modes["small", "b_shade"])` for shaded trees. With a
large one (`r f2(exp(shade_modes["large", "log_sd_field"]))`), each field gets its own
level, and the exponents describe mostly how biomass changes with diameter **within** a
field: `r f1(shade_modes["large", "b"])` for unshaded and
`r f1(shade_modes["large", "b"] + shade_modes["large", "b_shade"])` for shaded trees. The
second fit is better by `r f2(shade_modes["small", "nll"] - shade_modes["large", "nll"])`
log-likelihood units. The slopes of $\log(\mathrm{AGB})$ on $\log(D)$ within each field
(least squares, only to describe the data):

```{r}
within_slope = rep(NA, nlevels(main$field))
names(within_slope) = levels(main$field)
for (f in levels(main$field)) {
  trees_f = main[main$field == f, ]
  within_slope[f] = coef(lm(log(agb_kg) ~ log(dia20_cm), data = trees_f))[2]
}
round(within_slope, 2)
```

Within the CIV1 and ECU fields (unshaded, except CIV1_19), the biomass changes little with
the diameter (slopes from `r f2(min(within_slope[grepl("CIV1|ECU", names(within_slope))]))`
to `r f2(max(within_slope[grepl("CIV1|ECU", names(within_slope))]))`); within the CIV2
fields and the NGA fields of 12 and 47 years it changes with an exponent of about 2.5 to
3.
The fields have 3 to 9 trees and narrow ranges of diameter, so these slopes are noisy, and
an error in a diameter (D10, D14) flattens them; the ECU trees are also hedged at about
3 m, which may cap their biomass. Across fields, older fields have both thicker and much
heavier trees.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: a random effect on the level changes the meaning of the exponent"}
When the predictor varies mostly between groups (here the diameter between fields of
different ages), a random effect per group on the level lets the model explain the
differences between groups by the group effects, and the exponent then describes the
relation within groups. Whether it does depends on the estimated variance among groups,
and the likelihood can have one maximum for each interpretation. `optim()` reports
convergence at both, so the only signs are different results from different starting
values (Chapter 8) and a standard deviation among fields that jumps between candidates
(`sd_group` in the table). The estimates of the management effects depend on which
maximum is found.
:::

## Exponents within and between fields {#sec-field-mean}

The field mean of $\log(D/10)$, $\overline{L}_j$, as a predictor of $\log(a)$ separates the
two relations: $\log(\mu_{ij}) = \beta_{a,0} + \gamma\,\overline{L}_j + u_j + b\log(D_{ij}/10)$,
so $b$ is the exponent within fields and $b + \gamma$ the exponent between fields (for
trees typical of their field). It is a predictor of the field built with the model
matrix, so `allo_nll()` needs no change:

```{r}
add_field_mean = function(trees) {
  trees$log_dia_field = ave(log(trees$dia20_cm / 10), trees$field)
  trees
}
main = add_field_mean(main)
candidates_fm = list()
for (m in names(candidates)) {
  candidates_fm[[m]] = list(a = update(candidates[[m]]$a, ~ . + log_dia_field),
                            b = candidates[[m]]$b)
}
fm_fits = fit_candidates(main, candidates_fm)
fm_table = aic_table(fm_fits)
show_table(fm_table[, c("model", "K", "loglik", "convergence", "nll_gap", "sd_group",
                        "aic", "delta_aic")], digits = 1)
fm_none = summary(sdreport(fm_fits$none$obj), select = "fixed")
round(fm_none, 3)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
aic_fm = setNames(fm_table$aic, fm_table$model)
best_mgmt_fm = c("shade_b", "density_b", "shade_density_b")[
  which.min(aic_fm[c("shade_b", "density_b", "shade_density_b")])]
```

The field mean improves `none` by `r f1(aic_cand[["none"]] - aic_fm[["none"]])` AIC units
and `site_b` by `r f1(aic_cand[["site_b"]] - aic_fm[["site_b"]])`, and every candidate
now has a single maximum (`nll_gap` below
`r if (max(fm_table$nll_gap) < 0.001) "0.001" else f2(max(fm_table$nll_gap))`). Without
predictors, the exponent within fields is `r f2(fm_none["beta_b", 1])` and between fields
`r f2(fm_none["beta_b", 1] + fm_none[2, 1])`. The ranking of the candidates does not
change: `site_b` is `r f1(aic_fm[[best_mgmt_fm]] - aic_fm[["site_b"]])` AIC units better
than the best model with management only (`r best_mgmt_fm`). The term is a property of
the sample of trees in a field, so a prediction for a new tree needs the mean diameter of
its field; it is also close to a proxy for age. Whether the allometry of interest is the
relation within a stand or the relation along the development of stands is a question for
the author (and for the case study), and it changes the exponent more than any
management variable does.

# The answer: shaded and unshaded trees {#sec-answer}

The diameters of the answer must lie inside the data of both groups:

```{r}
tapply(main$dia20_cm, main$shade, range)
sort(main$dia20_cm[main$shade == "yes"])
```

The shaded trees cover `r min(main$dia20_cm[main$shade == "yes"])` to
`r max(main$dia20_cm[main$shade == "yes"])` cm, but with no tree between
`r max(main$dia20_cm[main$shade == "yes" & main$dia20_cm < 12])` and
`r min(main$dia20_cm[main$shade == "yes" & main$dia20_cm > 12])` cm: the small shaded trees
are all from CIV2 and the large ones from NGA and CIV1_19. We use 4 cm (inside the CIV2
trees and the youngest CIV1 and ECU trees) and 16 cm (inside the NGA, CIV1 and ECU_11
trees).

```{r}
answer_dia = c(4, 16)
shade_info = expand.grid(shade = factor(c("no", "yes"), levels = c("no", "yes")),
                         dia20_cm = answer_dia)
# Log ratio shaded/unshaded at each diameter.
shade_contrast = rbind(c(-1, 1, 0, 0), c(0, 0, -1, 1))
shade_info
shade_answer_setup = allo_setup(main, formulas = candidates$shade_b,
                                answer_info = shade_info,
                                answer_contrast = shade_contrast)
shade_fit = fit_allo(shade_answer_setup)
c(convergence = shade_fit$fit$convergence, nll_gap = shade_fit$nll_gap,
  sd_field = exp(shade_fit$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]]))
shade_answer = allo_answer(shade_fit, shade_info)
shade_ratio = allo_ratio(shade_fit, answer_dia)
show_table(shade_answer)
show_table(shade_ratio)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
ans_txt = function(tab, r) {
  paste0(f1(tab$agb_kg[r]), " kg (", f1(tab$lower[r]), " to ", f1(tab$upper[r]), ")")
}
ratio_txt = function(tab, r) {
  paste0(f2(tab$ratio[r]), " (", f2(tab$lower[r]), " to ", f2(tab$upper[r]), ")")
}
```

Under `shade_b` (at its better maximum), a typical unshaded tree of 4 cm has a mean
biomass of `r ans_txt(shade_answer, 1)` and a shaded one `r ans_txt(shade_answer, 2)`; at
16 cm the values are `r ans_txt(shade_answer, 3)` and `r ans_txt(shade_answer, 4)`. The
ratio shaded/unshaded is `r ratio_txt(shade_ratio, 1)` at 4 cm and
`r ratio_txt(shade_ratio, 2)` at 16 cm. Taken at face value, shaded trees are lighter
than unshaded ones at 4 cm and heavier at 16 cm, although the interval at 16 cm includes
1.

This fit lies at the maximum with a large variation among fields (standard deviation
`r f2(exp(shade_fit$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]]))`, @sec-two-maxima), where the exponent of
the unshaded trees, `r f2(shade_fit$fit$par[3])`, is mostly the slope within the CIV1 and
ECU fields. Its typical unshaded curve is the curve of a median field with that slope, and
the deviations of the fields (a factor of
`r f1(exp(exp(shade_fit$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]])))` for one standard deviation) carry
the rest, so the curve says little about how biomass grows from small to large unshaded
trees. @sec-sensitivity gives the ratios with the field mean of $\log(D/10)$ as a
predictor (@sec-field-mean), which separates the two slopes.

The same quantities per site, under `site_b`:

```{r}
site_info = expand.grid(site = factor(levels(main$site), levels = levels(main$site)),
                        dia20_cm = answer_dia)
site_fit = fit_allo(allo_setup(main, formulas = candidates$site_b,
                               answer_info = site_info))
c(convergence = site_fit$fit$convergence, nll_gap = site_fit$nll_gap,
  sd_field = exp(site_fit$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]]))
site_answer = allo_answer(site_fit, site_info)
# Is the diameter inside the range of the trees of the site?
site_min = tapply(main$dia20_cm, main$site, min)
site_max = tapply(main$dia20_cm, main$site, max)
site_answer$inside = site_answer$dia20_cm >= site_min[as.character(site_answer$site)] &
  site_answer$dia20_cm <= site_max[as.character(site_answer$site)]
site_answer$shade = c(CIV1 = "no (CIV1_19 yes)", CIV2 = "yes", ECU = "no",
                      NGA = "yes")[as.character(site_answer$site)]
show_table(site_answer[site_answer$inside, ])
site_b_par = site_fit$fit$par[names(site_fit$fit$par) == "beta_b"]
site_exponents = site_b_par[1] + c(0, site_b_par[-1])
names(site_exponents) = levels(main$site)
round(site_exponents, 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
sa = site_answer
sa_row = function(s, d) which(sa$site == s & sa$dia20_cm == d)
```

At 4 cm, only CIV1, CIV2 and ECU have trees around this diameter (NGA has none below
`r min(main$dia20_cm[main$site == "NGA"])` cm), and at 16 cm only CIV1, ECU and NGA (CIV2
has none above `r max(main$dia20_cm[main$site == "CIV2"])` cm). The "shade effect" at 4 cm
is therefore the difference between CIV2 (`r ans_txt(sa, sa_row("CIV2", 4))`) and CIV1
and ECU (`r ans_txt(sa, sa_row("CIV1", 4))` and `r ans_txt(sa, sa_row("ECU", 4))`), and
at 16 cm the difference between NGA (`r ans_txt(sa, sa_row("NGA", 16))`) and CIV1 and ECU
(`r ans_txt(sa, sa_row("CIV1", 16))` and `r ans_txt(sa, sa_row("ECU", 16))`). The
exponents of the sites under `site_b` range from `r f2(min(site_exponents))` to
`r f2(max(site_exponents))`; at this maximum of `site_b` the standard deviation among
fields is `r signif(exp(site_fit$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]]), 2)`, so the exponents are
those across fields.

**The answer, honestly.** The relation between diameter and biomass differs among sites,
and among fields within sites. Shaded and unshaded trees differ in these data, but the
shaded trees are the trees of CIV2 and NGA, and the difference is a difference between
sites; the data cannot attribute it to shade, density, irrigation or fertilisation rather
than to country, planting material, climate, age structure or collector. The only
contrasts within sites show no detectable effect of management (@sec-candidates).

## Figure 3 of the manuscript, redrawn {#sec-figure3}

@fig-answer shows the data with the typical curves of `shade_b` and of `site_b`, each
drawn only over the range of diameters of its group.

```{r}
#| label: fig-answer
#| fig-cap: "Aboveground biomass against stem diameter with typical curves (u = 0), each
#|   over the diameter range of its group: shaded (solid) and unshaded (dashed) trees
#|   under shade_b (top), and the four sites under site_b (bottom), on the original scale
#|   (left) and on logarithmic axes (right). Colours mark the sites, filled symbols the
#|   shaded trees."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7.5
curve_from_fit = function(fit, setup_formulas, info) {
  # Typical mean biomass for the rows of info (one row per diameter).
  par = fit$fit$par
  X_a = model.matrix(setup_formulas$a, data = info)
  X_b = model.matrix(setup_formulas$b, data = info)
  exp(X_a %*% par[names(par) == "beta_a"] +
        (X_b %*% par[names(par) == "beta_b"]) * log(info$dia20_cm / 10))
}
draw_panel = function(log_axes, groups, group_var, formulas, fit, ltys, cols) {
  plot(agb_kg ~ dia20_cm, data = main, log = if (log_axes) "xy" else "",
       col = site_colours[as.character(main$site)],
       pch = shade_symbols[as.character(main$shade)],
       xlab = "Stem diameter at 20 cm (cm)", ylab = "Aboveground biomass (kg)")
  for (g in seq_along(groups)) {
    in_group = main[[group_var]] == groups[g]
    dia = exp(seq(from = log(min(main$dia20_cm[in_group])),
                  to = log(max(main$dia20_cm[in_group])), length.out = 100))
    info = data.frame(dia20_cm = dia)
    info[[group_var]] = factor(groups[g], levels = levels(main[[group_var]]))
    lines(dia, curve_from_fit(fit, formulas, info), lty = ltys[g], col = cols[g],
          lwd = 2)
  }
}
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
for (log_axes in c(FALSE, TRUE)) {
  draw_panel(log_axes, c("no", "yes"), "shade", candidates$shade_b, shade_fit,
             ltys = c(2, 1), cols = c("black", "black"))
}
legend("topleft", legend = c("unshaded", "shaded"), lty = c(2, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
for (log_axes in c(FALSE, TRUE)) {
  draw_panel(log_axes, levels(main$site), "site", candidates$site_b, site_fit,
             ltys = rep(1, 4), cols = site_colours)
}
legend("topleft", legend = names(site_colours), col = site_colours, lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       bty = "n")
par(old_par)
```

The typical curve of the unshaded trees is much flatter than the unshaded trees
themselves: it lies above the smallest and far below the largest unshaded trees, because
at this maximum of `shade_b` it is the curve of a median field with the slope within
fields (@sec-two-maxima). The curve of the shaded trees passes through the CIV2 trees and
then the NGA trees, and bridges the gap between them, where there are no shaded trees.
The site curves cover different ranges of diameter and overlap only in part: at 4 cm the
ECU curve lies highest and the CIV2 curve lowest, at 16 cm the CIV1 curve lies above the
NGA and ECU curves (the table above), and the ECU curve is the flattest. The shade curves
join pieces of different site curves.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: predictions outside the data"}
Figure 3 of the manuscript draws curves for "low (1000 trees/ha) and high (1400
trees/ha)" planting densities with and without shade, from 0 to 32 cm. In the data,
shaded fields have 1,100, 1,111 or 1,333 trees/ha and unshaded fields 1,130, 1,333 or
1,500; no field has 1,000 or 1,400 trees/ha, and shaded trees at a high density do not
exist. Shaded trees between about 9 and 15 cm do not exist either. A model with
management predictors predicts for combinations of predictors and diameters, and both
must lie inside the data: the predictor space, not only the range of diameters, limits
what the model can say. Curves drawn only over the data of each group, as in
@fig-answer of this document, show this directly.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="For the author: the manuscript's scaled equation"}
The curves of the manuscript's Figure 3 cannot be reproduced reliably from its published
equation: the table of scaling constants of Supplement 2 labels its columns $\ln(\mathrm{CSA})$,
$\ln(\mathrm{dia20})$ and $\ln(\text{planting density})$, but the means 174.64 and
1209.66 are on the original scale; its formula for the cross-sectional area
($\mathrm{dia20}/2\times\pi$) is not an area; and the equation writes $\ln(\mathrm{dia}^2)$
and $\ln(\mathrm{dia}^3)$ for $(\ln \mathrm{dia})^2$ and $(\ln \mathrm{dia})^3$. This
document therefore does not redraw the manuscript's curves.
:::

# Checking the model {#sec-checks}

## Scaled quantile residuals {#sec-residuals}

We simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples from `shade_b` (new deviations of the fields, then
new biomasses) and compare each tree with the typical curve of its group.

```{r}
n_sim = 1000
shade_obj = shade_fit$obj
shade_par = shade_fit$fit$par
allo_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(main), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 2026)
for (s in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  allo_simulations[, s] = shade_obj$simulate(shade_par)$agb
}
shade_expected = as.vector(curve_from_fit(shade_fit, candidates$shade_b, main))

allo_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = allo_simulations,
  observedResponse = main$agb_kg,
  fittedPredictedResponse = shade_expected
)
```

`obj$simulate()` works with `dlnorm()` of RTMB, so no simulation by hand is needed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of shade_b, one per tree: quantile-quantile plot
#|   (left) and residuals against the (rank-transformed) typical mean (right)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
plot(allo_residuals)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma-site
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of shade_b, one per tree, against the site (left),
#|   and one per field (right) against the site of the field."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
field_index = as.numeric(main$field)
field_residuals = DHARMa::recalculateResiduals(allo_residuals, group = field_index)
field_site = factor(tapply(as.character(main$site), main$field, unique))
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
DHARMa::plotResiduals(allo_residuals, form = main$site)
DHARMa::plotResiduals(field_residuals, form = field_site)
par(old_par)
field_scaled = residuals(field_residuals)
names(field_scaled) = levels(main$field)
round(sort(field_scaled), 3)
```

The quantile-quantile plot follows the line: the LogNormal distribution with a random
effect per field describes the spread of the trees. Against the typical mean, the
residuals are low for the smallest predictions and high in the middle (DHARMa draws its
quantile curves in red): the flat typical curve of the unshaded trees lies above the
small and below the large unshaded trees (@fig-answer), and the deviations of the fields,
which the simulations draw anew, cannot follow the diameter. Against the site, the
residuals of the trees differ: the box of CIV2 lies below 0.5 and that of NGA (both
shaded) above, which is the difference between sites that the shade effect cannot absorb;
the CIV1 residuals spread over almost the whole range.
The residuals per field add up the trees of each field, and with 12 fields of 3 to 9 trees
they are rough. As in Chapter 6, the p-values that DHARMa prints on its plots are not used
for decisions: they test exact agreement, not whether the disagreement matters for the
question.

## The standard deviation among fields {#sec-profile}

The standard deviation among fields of the power law without predictors (@sec-choices),
with a likelihood profile interval calculated on the log scale and transformed back:

```{r}
power_profile_sd = TMB::tmbprofile(power_fit$obj, name = "log_sd_group", trace = FALSE)
sd_field_ci = exp(c(estimate = power_par[["log_sd_group"]],
                    confint(power_profile_sd)[1, ]))
sd_field_ci
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-profile
#| fig-cap: "Likelihood profile of the logarithm of the standard deviation among fields
#|   (power law without predictors), on the relative log-likelihood scale. The dashed line
#|   marks the cutoff of 1.92."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
plot(power_profile_sd$log_sd_group, -(power_profile_sd$value - power_fit$fit$value),
     type = "l", xlab = "log(standard deviation among fields)",
     ylab = "Relative log-likelihood")
abline(h = -1.92, lty = 2)
```

The standard deviation among fields is `r f2(sd_field_ci[1])` (profile interval
`r f2(sd_field_ci[2])` to `r f2(sd_field_ci[3])`) on the log scale of the biomass, against
`r f2(sigma_power)` among trees within a field. With 12 fields, the interval spans a
factor of about `r f0(sd_field_ci[3] / sd_field_ci[2])`. For `shade_b` and `site_b` a
profile of the same parameter is not useful: their likelihoods have two maxima in this
parameter (@sec-two-maxima), and one of them lies near zero, at the boundary.

The maximum likelihood estimate of a variance among few groups is biased downwards
(Chapter 7). REML integrates out the fixed effects as well:

```{r}
reml_models = c("none", "shade_b", "site_b")
reml_sd = matrix(NA, nrow = 3, ncol = 3,
                 dimnames = list(reml_models, c("ml", "reml", "reml_nll_gap")))
for (m in reml_models) {
  reml_fit = fit_allo(allo_setup(main, formulas = candidates[[m]]), reml = TRUE)
  reml_sd[m, ] = c(sd_cand[[m]], exp(reml_fit$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]]),
                   reml_fit$nll_gap)
}
round(reml_sd, 3)
```

Without predictors, REML gives `r f2(reml_sd["none", "reml"])` against
`r f2(reml_sd["none", "ml"])` by maximum likelihood. For `shade_b` and `site_b` the REML
estimates (`r f2(reml_sd["shade_b", "reml"])` and `r f2(reml_sd["site_b", "reml"])`) lie
at the maximum with a large variation among fields, whatever the maximum likelihood fit
chose: with 12 fields and 4 or 8 fixed effects, the information left for the variance
among fields is small.

## Sensitivity of the answer {#sec-sensitivity}

The comparison of the candidates and the answer under five variants: the main data set,
the `r nrow(manuscript_trees)` trees of the manuscript, the main data set with the
diameters of D10 and D14 exchanged, the main data set with the CIV1 field of 1.5 years
shaded (Table 1 of the manuscript), and the main data set with the field mean of
$\log(D/10)$ (@sec-field-mean). For each: the AIC of `shade_b`, `density_b` and
`shade_density_b` relative to `site_b` (positive means worse than the site), the
standard deviation among fields and `nll_gap` of `shade_b`, and the ratio shaded/unshaded
at 4 and 16 cm under `shade_b`.

```{r}
sensitivity_row = function(trees, field_mean = FALSE) {
  trees = add_field_mean(droplevels(trees))
  forms = candidates[c("shade_b", "density_b", "shade_density_b", "site_b")]
  info = shade_info
  if (field_mean) {
    for (m in names(forms)) {
      forms[[m]]$a = update(forms[[m]]$a, ~ . + log_dia_field)
    }
    # A tree typical of its field: the field mean equals its own log(D / 10).
    info$log_dia_field = log(info$dia20_cm / 10)
  }
  fits = list()
  for (m in names(forms)) {
    fits[[m]] = fit_allo(allo_setup(trees, formulas = forms[[m]]))
  }
  # Refit shade_b with the answer.
  fits$shade_b = fit_allo(allo_setup(trees, formulas = forms$shade_b, answer_info = info,
                                     answer_contrast = shade_contrast))
  tab = aic_table(fits)
  aic = setNames(tab$aic, tab$model)
  ratio = allo_ratio(fits$shade_b, answer_dia)
  data.frame(
    shade_b = aic[["shade_b"]] - aic[["site_b"]],
    density_b = aic[["density_b"]] - aic[["site_b"]],
    shade_density_b = aic[["shade_density_b"]] - aic[["site_b"]],
    sd_field = tab$sd_group[1], nll_gap = tab$nll_gap[1],
    ratio_4 = ratio$ratio[1], lower_4 = ratio$lower[1], upper_4 = ratio$upper[1],
    ratio_16 = ratio$ratio[2], lower_16 = ratio$lower[2], upper_16 = ratio$upper[2]
  )
}
swapped = main
swap_rows = match(c("D10", "D14"), swapped$tree)
swapped$dia20_cm[swap_rows] = swapped$dia20_cm[rev(swap_rows)]
civ1_shaded = main
civ1_shaded$shade[civ1_shaded$field == "CIV1_1.5"] = "yes"
sensitivity = rbind(
  main = sensitivity_row(main),
  manuscript_61 = sensitivity_row(manuscript_trees),
  swap_D10_D14 = sensitivity_row(swapped),
  CIV1_1.5_shaded = sensitivity_row(civ1_shaded),
  field_mean = sensitivity_row(main, field_mean = TRUE)
)
sensitivity = data.frame(variant = rownames(sensitivity), sensitivity)
show_table(sensitivity[, c("variant", "shade_b", "density_b", "shade_density_b",
                           "sd_field", "nll_gap")])
show_table(sensitivity[, c("variant", "ratio_4", "lower_4", "upper_4", "ratio_16",
                           "lower_16", "upper_16")])
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
sens = sensitivity
rownames(sens) = sens$variant
mgmt_cols = c("shade_b", "density_b", "shade_density_b")
sens_best = apply(sens[, mgmt_cols], 1, min)
```

The verdict of AIC depends on the variant. With the main data set, the 61 trees and the
field mean, the site on both parameters is better than every management model (by at least
`r f1(min(sens_best[c("main", "manuscript_61", "field_mean")]))` AIC units). With D10 and
D14 exchanged, `shade_density_b` is `r f1(-sens["swap_D10_D14", "shade_density_b"])`
units better than `site_b`, and with the CIV1 field of 1.5 years shaded, the best
management model is `r f1(sens_best[["CIV1_1.5_shaded"]])` units behind the site. The
ratio shaded/unshaded at 4 cm ranges from `r f2(min(sens$ratio_4))` to
`r f2(max(sens$ratio_4))` and at 16 cm from `r f2(min(sens$ratio_16))` to
`r f2(max(sens$ratio_16))` across the variants, and the standard deviation among fields of
`shade_b` from `r signif(min(sens$sd_field), 2)` to `r f2(max(sens$sd_field))`. Two
uncertain diameters, one disputed description of a field and the choice between two maxima
of the likelihood decide whether management "explains" the allometry: the data cannot
carry the conclusion.

# Extension: height and diameter {#sec-height}

Supplement 3 of the manuscript shows that shaded trees are more slender (taller for their
diameter). The height of a tree cannot grow without bound with its diameter, so a
saturating curve is a natural model, non-linear in its parameters and with a random effect
per field: the saturating exponential (functions supplement, `sec-fn-monomolecular`),

$$
h(D) = H_{\max}\left(1 - e^{-D/s}\right),
$$

where $H_{\max}$ is the asymptotic height (m) and $s$ (cm) the diameter at which the
height reaches $1 - e^{-1} \approx 63\%$ of $H_{\max}$; the initial slope is $H_{\max}/s$
(m/cm). The Michaelis–Menten function $H_{\max}D/(s + D)$, with $s$ the half-maximum,
is the alternative curve. The random effect per field and the predictors act on
$\log(H_{\max})$; $s$ is shared.

```{r}
height_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  height = OBS(height)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the fields, before they are used.
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_group), log = TRUE))
  h_max = exp(X_h %*% beta_h + u[group])
  s = exp(log_s)
  if (curve == "exponential") {
    mu = h_max * (1 - exp(-dia / s))
  } else {
    mu = h_max * dia / (s + dia)
  }
  # Minus the log density of the heights for given deviations.
  if (distribution == "LogNormal") {
    sdlog = exp(log_disp)
    nll = nll - sum(dlnorm(x = height, meanlog = log(mu) - sdlog^2 / 2, sdlog = sdlog,
                           log = TRUE))
  } else if (distribution == "Gamma") {
    shape = exp(log_disp)
    nll = nll - sum(dgamma(x = height, shape = shape, scale = mu / shape, log = TRUE))
  } else {
    nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = height, mean = mu, sd = exp(log_disp), log = TRUE))
  }
  nll
}
height_setup = function(trees, formula = ~ 1, curve = "exponential",
                        distribution = "LogNormal") {
  data = list(height = trees$height_m, dia = trees$dia20_cm, curve = curve,
              distribution = distribution, random = "field",
              X_h = model.matrix(formula, data = trees),
              group = as.numeric(droplevels(trees$field)))
  start = list(beta_h = c(log(7), rep(0, ncol(data$X_h) - 1)), log_s = log(10),
               log_disp = switch(distribution, LogNormal = log(0.1), Gamma = log(100),
                                 Normal = log(0.5)),
               log_sd_group = log(0.3), u = rep(0, nlevels(droplevels(trees$field))))
  list(data = data, start = start)
}
```

The starting values come from @fig-scatter and the heights in the data: trees approach
about 7 m, and reach most of it by about 10 cm. First the curve and the distribution,
without predictors:

```{r}
height_choices = expand.grid(curve = c("exponential", "michaelis_menten"),
                             distribution = c("LogNormal", "Gamma", "Normal"),
                             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
height_choice_fits = list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(height_choices))) {
  setup = height_setup(main, curve = height_choices$curve[i],
                       distribution = height_choices$distribution[i])
  height_choice_fits[[i]] = fit_allo(setup, nll = height_nll)
}
names(height_choice_fits) = paste(height_choices$curve, height_choices$distribution)
height_choice_table = aic_table(height_choice_fits)
show_table(height_choice_table, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
hc = height_choice_table
hc_best = hc$model[which.min(hc$aic)]
hc_best_curve = height_choices$curve[which.min(hc$aic)]
hc_best_dist = height_choices$distribution[which.min(hc$aic)]
curve_names = c(exponential = "saturating exponential",
                michaelis_menten = "Michaelis–Menten")
```

`r if (all(hc$convergence == 0)) "All six fits converged." else "Not every fit converged (see the table)."`
The best combination is the `r curve_names[[hc_best_curve]]`
curve with the `r hc_best_dist` distribution. With this curve, the other two
distributions are both about
`r f1(max(hc$delta_aic[height_choices$curve == hc_best_curve]))` AIC units worse, and the
other curve is `r f1(min(hc$delta_aic[height_choices$curve != hc_best_curve]))` units
behind at best, so the two curves describe the heights about equally well. Heights range
only from `r min(main$height_m)` to `r max(main$height_m)` m, a much narrower range than
the biomasses, and a constant variance is enough here.
Then the predictors of $H_{\max}$, with this curve and distribution:

```{r}
height_candidates = list(none = ~ 1, shade = ~ shade, density = ~ density_100,
                         irrigation = ~ irrigation, site = ~ site)
height_fits = list()
for (m in names(height_candidates)) {
  height_fits[[m]] = fit_allo(height_setup(main, formula = height_candidates[[m]],
                                           curve = hc_best_curve,
                                           distribution = hc_best_dist),
                              nll = height_nll)
}
height_table = aic_table(height_fits)
show_table(height_table, digits = 1)
height_site = height_fits$site$fit$par
site_hmax = exp(height_site[names(height_site) == "beta_h"][1] +
                  c(0, height_site[names(height_site) == "beta_h"][-1]))
names(site_hmax) = levels(main$site)
round(c(site_hmax, s_cm = exp(height_site[["log_s"]])), 2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
aic_h = setNames(height_table$aic, height_table$model)
height_shade = summary(sdreport(height_fits$shade$obj), select = "fixed")
```

`r if (all(height_table$convergence == 0)) "All five fits converged." else "Not every fit converged (see the table)."`
The site is `r f1(aic_h[["none"]] - aic_h[["site"]])` AIC units better than no predictor
and `r f1(min(aic_h[c("shade", "density", "irrigation")]) - aic_h[["site"]])` units better
than the best management variable,
`r c("shade", "density", "irrigation")[which.min(aic_h[c("shade", "density", "irrigation")])]`
(irrigation is "yes" exactly at CIV2 and ECU). The typical asymptotic heights of the sites are
`r paste(paste0(names(site_hmax), " ", f1(site_hmax), " m"), collapse = ", ")`: the
hedged ECU trees are no taller than
`r max(main$height_m[main$site == "ECU"])` m. Shade multiplies $H_{\max}$ by
`r f2(exp(height_shade[2, 1]))` (95% Wald interval
`r f2(exp(height_shade[2, 1] - critical_value * height_shade[2, 2]))` to
`r f2(exp(height_shade[2, 1] + critical_value * height_shade[2, 2]))`), but the
unshaded trees include the hedged ECU trees, so this is again largely a difference
between sites, and hedging limits the height of the ECU trees.

```{r}
#| label: fig-height
#| fig-cap: "Height against stem diameter with the typical curves (u = 0) of the four
#|   sites under the height model with the site on the asymptotic height, each over the
#|   diameter range of its site."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
height_curve = function(dia, h_max, s) {
  if (hc_best_curve == "exponential") h_max * (1 - exp(-dia / s)) else h_max * dia / (s + dia)
}
plot(height_m ~ dia20_cm, data = main, col = site_colours[as.character(main$site)],
     pch = shade_symbols[as.character(main$shade)],
     xlab = "Stem diameter at 20 cm (cm)", ylab = "Height (m)")
for (s in levels(main$site)) {
  dia = seq(from = site_min[[s]], to = site_max[[s]], length.out = 100)
  lines(dia, height_curve(dia, site_hmax[[s]], exp(height_site[["log_s"]])),
        col = site_colours[[s]], lwd = 2)
}
legend("bottomright", legend = names(site_colours), col = site_colours, lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       bty = "n")
```

The ECU curve lies lowest over its whole range and is nearly flat beyond about 15 cm;
the NGA trees are the tallest, and the CIV1 and CIV2 curves lie between. The slenderness of the shaded trees in the
manuscript's Supplement 3 is, in these data, mostly the contrast between hedged ECU trees
and the trees of the other sites.

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative: height in the biomass model"}
The manuscript's equation 3 adds $\log(H)$ to the log-log regression, and its Table 5
shows a large improvement. Height is a response of the tree to its environment and
management (pruning, shade), so including it answers a different question (biomass for a
given diameter and height); it may also explain why biomass changes little with diameter
within the hedged ECU fields (@sec-two-maxima).
:::

# Checking the estimator by simulation {#sec-simulation}

With 12 fields, can the data detect a shade effect, and are the Wald intervals of the
ratio shaded/unshaded reliable? We simulate 250 hypothetical samples from the power law
without predictors (@sec-choices), in which shade has no effect, with the trees,
diameters and fields of the main data set, and fit `none` and `shade_b` to each. We keep
whether the 95% Wald interval of the log ratio at 4 and 16 cm contains zero (the value
used to simulate), whether AIC prefers `shade_b` by more than 2 units, the standard
deviation among fields of `shade_b` and its `nll_gap`.

```{r}
n_samples = 250
sim_setup_none = allo_setup(main)
sim_setup_shade = shade_answer_setup
sim_covered = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 2)
sim_prefers_shade = rep(NA, n_samples)
sim_sd_field = rep(NA, n_samples)
sim_gap = rep(NA, n_samples)
n_failed = 0
set.seed(seed = 1932)
for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
  agb_sim = power_fit$obj$simulate(power_par)$agb
  sim_setup_none$data$agb = agb_sim
  sim_setup_shade$data$agb = agb_sim
  sim_none = fit_allo(sim_setup_none)
  sim_shade = fit_allo(sim_setup_shade)
  n_failed = n_failed + (sim_none$fit$convergence != 0) +
    (sim_shade$fit$convergence != 0)
  log_ratio = report_rows(sim_shade, "log_ratio")
  sim_covered[i, ] = abs(log_ratio[, "Estimate"]) <
    critical_value * log_ratio[, "Std. Error"]
  aic_none = 2 * length(sim_none$fit$par) + 2 * sim_none$fit$value
  aic_shade = 2 * length(sim_shade$fit$par) + 2 * sim_shade$fit$value
  sim_prefers_shade[i] = aic_shade < aic_none - 2
  sim_sd_field[i] = exp(sim_shade$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]])
  sim_gap[i] = sim_shade$nll_gap
}
n_failed
c(coverage_4 = mean(sim_covered[, 1]), coverage_16 = mean(sim_covered[, 2]),
  prefers_shade = mean(sim_prefers_shade), two_maxima = mean(sim_gap > 0.05),
  sd_near_zero = mean(sim_sd_field < 0.01))
summary(sim_sd_field)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
cov_lo = 0.95 - 1.96 * sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / n_samples)
```

`r if (n_failed == 0) "Every fit converged." else paste(n_failed, "fits did not converge.")`
Although shade has no effect in the simulated data, the 95% Wald intervals of the ratio
contain 1 in `r f1(100 * mean(sim_covered[, 1]))`% of the samples at 4 cm and
`r f1(100 * mean(sim_covered[, 2]))`% at 16 cm
(`r if (max(colMeans(sim_covered)) < cov_lo) "both below" else "against"` the lower limit
of about `r f1(100 * cov_lo)`% that `r n_samples` samples allow for a coverage of 95%), and
AIC prefers `shade_b` over `none` by more than 2 units in
`r f1(100 * mean(sim_prefers_shade))`% of the samples. In
`r f1(100 * mean(sim_gap > 0.05))`% of the samples the fit of `shade_b` has two maxima, and
in `r f1(100 * mean(sim_sd_field < 0.01))`% the standard deviation among fields goes to
practically zero; its median is `r f2(median(sim_sd_field))` against
`r f2(sd_field_power)` used to simulate. With 6 shaded and 6 unshaded fields, the
variation among fields is underestimated, and with it the uncertainty of an effect that
is a contrast between fields.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the number of fields, not of trees"}
A management effect that is constant within fields is estimated from the
`r nlevels(main$field)` fields, not from the `r nrow(main)` trees, and with so few groups
the Wald intervals are too narrow and the variance among fields is
underestimated (@sec-simulation, @sec-profile). Here the shaded and unshaded fields also belong to
different sites, which no simulation from the model can repair.
:::

# Summary: alternatives, pitfalls and teaching notes {#sec-summary}

**Answer.** On logarithmic axes, the aboveground biomass of cocoa trees is close to a
straight line of the stem diameter (a power law with exponent
`r f2(power_par[["beta_b"]])` across all fields; a LogNormal distribution with a
standard deviation of `r f2(sigma_power)` on the log scale and a random effect per field
with a standard deviation of `r f2(sd_field_power)`). Shaded and unshaded trees differ:
under `shade_b`, the ratio shaded/unshaded of the typical mean biomass is
`r ratio_txt(shade_ratio, 1)` at 4 cm and `r ratio_txt(shade_ratio, 2)` at 16 cm. But the
site on both parameters of the power law fits better than any management variable, the
small shaded trees are all from CIV2 and the large ones from NGA, the only contrasts
within sites show no detectable effect of management, and the verdict of AIC changes with
two uncertain diameters and one disputed field description. The data show that the
allometry differs among sites and fields; they cannot attribute the differences to shade,
planting density, irrigation or fertilisation.

**Pitfalls.**

1. Management is almost a property of the site; only three small contrasts lie within
   sites (@sec-design).
2. Three records are implausible by a simple form factor (F9, D4, D5), and five more do
   not add up or look swapped (T17, F11 and F12, D10 and D14) (@sec-records).
3. The descriptions of fields disagree between Table 1 and the spreadsheet (shade in
   CIV1_1.5; the two CIV2 fields may be one) (@sec-design).
4. A Normal distribution with constant variance is far worse than a LogNormal or Gamma
   one (@sec-choices).
5. A line fitted to the logarithm of the biomass describes the median; the LogNormal with
   its mean as a parameter needs no correction factor (@sec-model).
6. A cubic polynomial of $\log(D)$ turns down within or near the data, and its curvature
   comes from D4 and D5 (@sec-cubic).
7. The site fits better than any management variable; the manuscript never compared
   them (@sec-candidates).
8. The likelihood of several candidates has two maxima, one with little variation among
   fields (exponents across fields) and one with much (exponents within fields), and
   `optim()` reports convergence at both (@sec-two-maxima).
9. The exponent within fields (`r f2(fm_none["beta_b", 1])`) differs from that between
   fields (`r f2(fm_none["beta_b", 1] + fm_none[2, 1])`) (@sec-field-mean).
10. Predictions must stay inside the data in diameter and in the combinations of
    predictors; the manuscript's scenarios of 1,000 and 1,400 trees/ha with shade lie
    outside (@sec-figure3).
11. With 12 fields, Wald intervals of a contrast between fields are too narrow and AIC
    finds a shade effect that does not exist in about
    `r f0(100 * mean(sim_prefers_shade))`% of simulated samples (@sec-simulation).
12. Shade appears to make trees taller, but the unshaded trees include the hedged ECU
    trees (@sec-height).

**Alternatives.**

- The Gamma distribution, or a Normal distribution with variance as a power of the mean
  (same fit; @sec-choices).
- The field mean of $\log(D/10)$ as a predictor, which separates the exponents within and
  between fields and removes the second maximum (@sec-field-mean).
- Nested random effects of site and field (@sec-choices; beyond Chapter 7).
- REML for the variance among fields (@sec-profile).
- Height as a second predictor of biomass, for a different question (@sec-height).
- A monotonic curve with a bend instead of a polynomial, if a bend is needed (@sec-cubic).

**Teaching notes (possible questions for students).**

- Calculate the form factor and decide which records are implausible, and say what the
  decision does to the answer.
- Explain why the LogNormal mean differs from the curve of a log-log regression, and
  connect it to the "correction factor".
- Compare a random effect per field and per site, and explain what each assumes about the
  trees.
- Fit the cubic of the manuscript and find where it turns.
- Compare management with the site as a fixed effect, and explain what the comparison
  says about the research question.
- Fit `shade_b` from different starting values of the standard deviation among fields,
  and explain the two maxima.
- Redraw the manuscript's Figure 3 with each curve over the data of its group.
